comparison: Perfect agreement on C73-C74. Both acknowledge the trend suggesting hybridization does not increase transposition and appropriately note the limitation of small sample sizes for statistical testing. OpenEval emphasizes the statistical limitation while peer review confirms this aligns with previous results.

Perfect agreement on C125-C127. Both strongly support the central conclusion that structural variation rather than transposition shapes TE copy number evolution. This represents the main finding of the paper with explicit support from all reviewers.

Strong agreement on C54-C60 regarding statistical correlations between Ty CN and genome size changes. Both find the mixed linear models and correlation analyses well-supported. Peer review emphasizes this supports the major conclusion about structural variation driving TE load changes.

Strong agreement on C87-C88 regarding mtDNA influence on transposition rates. Both support the reciprocal cross data and directional effects. OpenEval characterizes the effect as moderate while peer review calls it intriguing and worthy of future exploration.

Strong agreement on C61-C66 regarding de novo insertion identification and validation. Both support the rigorous filtering criteria and low number of insertions (18 total, 0.14 per line). This finding is central to the conclusion that transposition plays only a minor role.

Strong agreement on C77-C80 regarding transposition rate measurements in SpB. Both support the quantitative fluctuation assay data and steep negative relationship with copy number. Peer review also addresses broader genotype-specific factors (C90-C91) that OpenEval evaluates separately.

Strong agreement on C81-C83 regarding Ty1 variant-specific transposition rates. Both support the comparative data across variants. Peer review explicitly notes this as a novel finding not previously tested by others. OpenEval also addresses C84 (hybrid intermediate rates) which peer review evaluates separately.

Substantial agreement on C47-C50, C53 regarding classification results and SV types. Both support the quantitative findings (89.8% classified, 79% unchanged). Peer review groups these with broader claims about structural variation's role (C6, C89) while OpenEval focuses specifically on the classification methodology and results.

Agreement on C34-C35, C42-C43 regarding sequencing approach and assembly quality. Both support the technical quality of the work. Peer review emphasizes the non-trivial effort and novel insights from long-read sequencing, while OpenEval focuses on internal consistency and classification rate explanations.

Agreement on C84 regarding intermediate transposition rates in hybrids. Both support this as evidence for robust TE regulation. OpenEval emphasizes this supports robust regulation with citations, while peer review notes consistency with the overall conclusion that hybridization does not trigger TE reactivation.

Partial overlap on C97-C98 regarding SpC-specific effects. OpenEval finds these claims supported but notes an unresolved paradox (C96, C99-C100). Peer review focuses on the novel finding of Ty1 sequence-specific effects (C81-C83) and does not specifically address the paradox OpenEval identifies.

Partial overlap on C90-C91. Both support that in vivo assays demonstrate genotype-specific factors affect transposition rates and confirm previous work. OpenEval groups these with C89 as major findings summary, while peer review emphasizes the broader conclusion about hybridization not increasing transposition.

Minimal overlap on C99 regarding mtDNA effects in SpC context. OpenEval addresses this as part of the SpC-specific paradox (C96-C100), while peer review evaluates mtDNA effects more generally (C87-C88). Both find the data supported but focus on different aspects.

Minimal overlap on C89. OpenEval includes this in a summary of major findings (C89-C91), while peer review groups it with specific structural variation claims (C6, C47-C50, C53). Both support the conclusion but in different contexts.

OpenEval evaluates C69-C70 regarding phylogenetic analyses and horizontal transfer interpretation. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims about global Ty1 activity and phylogenetic distribution.

OpenEval evaluates C71-C72 regarding specific insertion events and AIM29 disruption with detailed sequence characterization. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific insertion characterizations.

OpenEval evaluates C92-C93 regarding interpretations of SV impacts on TE load and speculation about selection efficiency in MA experiments. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific interpretive claims.

OpenEval evaluates C103-C105 identifying the discrepancy between MA-derived and in vivo rate estimates. Finds the observation well-supported but explanation speculative. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this discrepancy.

OpenEval rates C106-C111 as UNCERTAIN, noting the adenine starvation hypothesis is speculative and represents an important limitation requiring future work. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses this potential confounding factor.

OpenEval evaluates C112-C114 regarding SpB data interpretation in light of copy number control (CNC) mechanisms, noting the evidence is correlative. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses CNC interpretation.

OpenEval rates C115-C117 as UNCERTAIN, noting that speculation about CNC dysfunction in SpC lacks direct molecular evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses this specific mechanistic speculation.

OpenEval evaluates C118-C121 regarding p22 sequence analysis and conservation, noting functional expression requires experimental validation. No corresponding peer review evaluation addresses these specific molecular details.
